title: Will and Cipher
premise: When the coffin of Harlan Voss, the town's beloved founder, is exhumed for a cemetery relocation and found empty, night-shift taxi dispatcher Ansel Pemberton realizes the fare logs he's kept for a decade contain a pattern no one else noticed: a cab that ran the same impossible route every year on the anniversary of Voss's death. The witness everyone swears is dead—Voss's former secretary, Edith Crane—is alive, hidden in plain sight, and she knows the founder's fortune was built on a buried crime. As Ansel closes in, the town's ruling families close in on him, and he must choose between exposing the truth and protecting the one person whose survival depends on the lie. In the end, Ansel delivers the evidence not to the police but to the town itself, letting justice arrive sideways, outside the law.
about_author: Zephyrine Delacroix is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper archivist who spent years reading decades of police blotters and obituaries, and never quite trusted either. They write mysteries about people who watch their towns too closely.

chapters.title: The Empty Box
chapters.summary: Ansel Pemberton, night dispatcher and professional invisible man, hears on the scanner that Harlan Voss's coffin has been exhumed for the cemetery move—and found empty. His POV establishes his pride in knowing every secret that passes through his dispatch board. The emotional beat is a cold thrill: for the first time, a mystery touches him personally.

chapters.title: Fare Log, Page One
chapters.summary: Ansel pulls his decade of dispatch logs and finds the anomaly: a cab dispatched to the Voss mausoleum every October 14th at 3 a.m., cash only, no return trip. POV shifts to Deputy Cora Ruiz, who resents being assigned to a case the mayor wants closed quietly. The beat is quiet dread—two watchers beginning to orbit the same secret.

chapters.title: The Widow's Smile
chapters.summary: Ansel interviews Voss's widow, Lucille, whose grief is immaculate and rehearsed. She slips once: she refers to a witness 'who died' with a tense that doesn't fit. Ansel's POV carries his growing conviction that the town's grief is a performance. The emotional beat is the first taste of power: he knows something the powerful don't know he knows.

chapters.title: Night Shift
chapters.summary: A slice of Ansel's world: the drivers, the drunks, the 4 a.m. confessions. A driver named Bo mentions picking up an old woman near the mausoleum years ago—paid in pre-decimal coins. Ansel's invisibility becomes an asset as drivers talk freely around him. The beat is warmth and loneliness intertwined; the dispatch desk is both his shield and his cage.

chapters.title: Edith Crane, Deceased
chapters.summary: Cora, working off the books, locates the death certificate of Edith Crane, Voss's secretary—signed by a doctor who died before the date on the certificate. Her POV reveals pressure from above to bury the file. The beat is professional conscience versus institutional loyalty, and conscience is winning.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Route
chapters.summary: Ansel stakes out the mausoleum on October 14th and watches a cab arrive—dispatched by his own board, by a shift he doesn't remember scheduling. Someone inside the company is complicit. His POV turns paranoid; the beat is the vertigo of realizing your own tools have been used against you.

chapters.title: Voss and the Water
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter: 1961, Edith Crane's POV, typing minutes of a board meeting where Voss and the founding families decide to bury a worker's death in the reservoir collapse—and the man who saw it happen. The beat is the origin of the lie, rendered with terrible bureaucratic calm.

chapters.title: A Fare to the Reservoir
chapters.summary: Ansel follows the old route to the drowned town site under the reservoir and finds a maintenance shack with fresh footprints and a tin of Edith's brand of tea. Cora, tailing him, confronts him; they form an uneasy alliance. The beat is trust extended cautiously between two people who trust no one.

chapters.title: The Company Speaks
chapters.summary: Ansel is offered a promotion and a raise by the taxi company's owner, Aldous Merritt—a founding-family scion—if he hands over his dispatch logs. His POV registers the offer as a confession. The beat is temptation made polite, and the pleasure of refusing it.

chapters.title: What Lucille Keeps
chapters.summary: Cora searches the Voss estate under a welfare-check pretext and finds Lucille burning papers—among them a photograph of Edith Crane taken after her 'death.' Lucille, cornered, admits she has been paying for Edith's silence for forty years. The beat is pity: even the widow is a prisoner of the lie.

chapters.title: The Witness Everyone Swears Is Dead
chapters.summary: Ansel finally meets Edith Crane in the reservoir shack—sharp, unrepentant, dying of a heart condition. She explains she faked her death to survive and has kept the ledger of the founding families' crimes as insurance. The beat is awe and fear: the truth is real, and holding it is lethal.

chapters.title: Ledger of the Founders
chapters.summary: Edith gives Ansel a copy of the ledger: bribes, the reservoir cover-up, and the fact that Voss's coffin was emptied by the families themselves to hide that he was never in it—he fled before his own exposure. Ansel's POV shifts from curiosity to responsibility. The beat is the weight of becoming the archive.

chapters.title: Tail Lights
chapters.summary: Someone ransacks Ansel's apartment and takes his original logs; Bo the driver is run off the road and hospitalized. Cora discovers the police chief has been feeding the families her case notes. The beat is grief and rage—the watcher learns what it costs to be seen.

chapters.title: The Dispatcher's Gambit
chapters.summary: Ansel realizes the thieves took copies of logs, not his memory—he kept a second ledger in the dispatch code only he can read. He and Edith decode it together, mapping the families' payments. The beat is quiet triumph: the invisible man's obsessive record-keeping becomes a weapon.

chapters.title: Merritt's Offer, Revised
chapters.summary: Merritt stops being polite: threats against Edith, against Cora's career, against Ansel's drivers. Ansel's POV registers fear for the first time and refuses to let it rule him. The beat is the corruption of power shown from the receiving end—power as a fist in a velvet glove.

chapters.title: Edith Fades
chapters.summary: Edith's heart fails; in the hospital under a false name, she entrusts Ansel with the original ledger and her testimony, recorded. Cora arranges protection but knows the hospital is a trap. The beat is tenderness under pressure—the dying witness passing the torch.

chapters.title: The Anniversary, Again
chapters.summary: On October 14th, the families move to erase Edith permanently; Ansel, watching his board, spots the fake dispatch order and reroutes their hired cab into a police checkpoint Cora has quietly set. The beat is the dispatcher's craft turned to salvation—every trick they used, used back.

chapters.title: What the Town Deserves
chapters.summary: Cora wants to take the ledger to the district attorney; Ansel argues the courts here belong to the families. They fight over what justice means. The beat is the book's moral crux: justice inside the law, or justice that works?

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Ansel chooses both: Cora files the legal case while Ansel reads the ledger, page by page, over the taxi company's own dispatch frequency on the night of the founder's day parade—every cab, every scanner, every kitchen radio in town. The beat is catharsis; the invisible man becomes the town's voice.

chapters.title: The Fall of the Families
chapters.summary: Merritt is arrested at the parade; Lucille publicly corroborates the ledger, choosing truth at last. The chief resigns. Cora's POV shows the machinery of official justice finally moving—because the ground was prepared outside it. The beat is vindication without triumphalism.

chapters.title: Edith's Grave
chapters.summary: Edith dies peacefully and is buried under her own name beside the reservoir, with the whole town watching. Ansel, who attended no one's funeral in ten years, carries her flowers. The beat is mourning transformed into restoration—names given back to the erased.

chapters.title: Night Shift, Page One
chapters.summary: Months later, Ansel is still at the dispatch desk, but the town now greets him by name; a new fare log begins on a clean page. Cora visits with coffee and an unsolved case. The beat is quiet hope: invisibility was a choice, and he chooses, now and then, to be seen.
